The '''57th Academy Awards''' ceremony, organized by the [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS), honored [[1984 in film|films released in 1984]] and took place on March 25, 1985, at the [[Dorothy Chandler Pavilion]] in Los Angeles. During the ceremony, AMPAS presented [[Academy Awards]] (commonly referred to as Oscars) in 23 categories. The ceremony, televised in the United States by [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], was produced by [[Gregory Peck]], [[Robert Wise]], [[Larry Gelbart]], and [[Gene Allen (art director)|Gene Allen]], and was directed by [[Marty Pasetta]].<ref name="Pasetta">{{harvnb|Osborne|2013|p=413}}</ref> Actor [[Jack Lemmon]] hosted the show for the fourth time. He first co-hosted the [[30th Academy Awards|30th ceremony]] held in 1958, and had last co-hosted the [[44th Academy Awards|44th ceremony]] in 1972.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Trott |first1=William C. |title=Glimpses |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/01/31/GLIMPSES/1550475995600/ |access-date=October 1, 2024 |work=[[United Press International]] |date=January 31, 1985 |archive-date=November 26, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241126223951/https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/01/31/GLIMPSES/1550475995600/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Sundby |first1=Alex |title=Who Hosted the 2024 Oscars, and Who Hosted Past Academy Awards Ceremonies? |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/oscars-host-2024/ |access-date=October 2, 2024 |agency=[[CBS News]] |date=March 10, 2024 |archive-date=August 31, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240831133808/https://www.cbsnews.com/news/oscars-host-2024/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

''[[Amadeus (film)|Amadeus]]'' won eight awards, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sharbutt |first1=Jay |title=''Amadeus'' Top Film; Field and Abraham Win |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-03-26-mn-28744-story.html |access-date=October 1, 2024 |url-access=subscription |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=March 26, 1985 |archive-date=June 9, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230609072755/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-03-26-mn-28744-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Other winners included ''[[The Killing Fields (film)|The Killing Fields]]'' with three awards, ''[[A Passage to India (film)|A Passage to India]]'' and ''[[Places in the Heart]]'' with two, and ''[[Charade (1984 film)|Charade]]'', ''[[Dangerous Moves]]'', ''[[Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom]]'', ''[[Purple Rain (film)|Purple Rain]]'', ''[[The Stone Carvers (film)|The Stone Carvers]]'', ''[[The Times of Harvey Milk]]'', ''[[Up (1984 film)|Up]]'', and ''[[The Woman in Red (1984 film)|The Woman in Red]]'' with one. The telecast was watched by an audience of 38.9&nbsp;million viewers. 

==Winners and nominees==
The nominees for the 57th Academy Awards were announced on February 6, 1985, by Academy president [[Gene Allen (art director)|Gene Allen]] and actress [[Eva Marie Saint]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Thomas |first1=Bob |title=Race for Oscars Has No Dominant Favorite |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-star-57th-oscar-nominat/166619939/ |access-date=January 23, 2025 |work=[[The Indianapolis Star]] |publisher=[[Associated Press]] |date=February 6, 1985 |page=55 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> ''[[Amadeus (film)|Amadeus]]'' and ''[[A Passage to India (film)|A Passage to India]]'' led all nominees with eleven each.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Pollock |first1=Dale |title=''Amadeus'' and ''A Passage to India'' Lead Oscar Derby |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-02-06-mn-4323-story.html |access-date=March 2, 2024 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url-access=subscription |date=February 6, 1985 |archive-date=January 19, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230119050040/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-02-06-mn-4323-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The winners were announced at the awards ceremony on March 25. [[Haing S. Ngor]] was the first Asian winner for [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor|Best Supporting Actor]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hilly |first1=Libby |title=Ke Huy Quan Is the First Asian Performer to Win the Best Supporting Actor Oscar in 38 Years |url=https://www.thewrap.com/ke-huy-quan-best-supporting-actor-oscar-win-record/ |access-date=October 2, 2024 |work=[[TheWrap]] |date=March 12, 2023 |archive-date=August 11, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240811083223/https://www.thewrap.com/ke-huy-quan-best-supporting-actor-oscar-win-record/ |url-status=live }}</ref> At age 77, [[Peggy Ashcroft]] became the oldest [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress|Best Supporting Actress]] winner.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Warren |first1=Jess |title=Dame Peggy Ashcroft Remembered with Blue Plaque |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cqllwq0z1dyo |access-date=October 2, 2024 |agency=[[BBC News]] |date=June 13, 2024 |archive-date=June 28, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240628015730/https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cqllwq0z1dyo |url-status=live }}</ref> Best Original Song winner [[Stevie Wonder]] was the first [[Visual impairment|blind]] person to win an Oscar.<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=1148}}</ref> For the first time in Oscar history, all five nominees for Best Original Song had reached the [[Lists of Billboard number-one singles|number-one spot]] on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] singles chart.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Collis |first1=Clark |title=Oscars' Best Song Race: Out of Tune? |url=https://ew.com/article/2010/02/05/oscars-best-song-race-out-tune/ |access-date=March 2, 2024 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |date=February 5, 2010 |archive-date=June 3, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230603202417/https://ew.com/article/2010/02/05/oscars-best-song-race-out-tune/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Ceremony information ==
[[File:Jack Lemmon 1988 ArM (cropped).jpg|thumb|alt=Jack Lemmon in 1988|[[Jack Lemmon]] hosted the 57th Academy Awards.]]
Determined to revive interest surrounding the awards and reverse declining ratings, the Academy recruited a four-person committee in December 1984 composed of actor [[Gregory Peck]], director [[Robert Wise]], screenwriter [[Larry Gelbart]], and AMPAS president [[Gene Allen (art director)|Gene Allen]] to oversee producing duties.<ref name="Producers">{{cite news |last1=Fox |first1=David |title=Outtakes: Terms of Endurance |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-terms-of-endurance/166681886/ |access-date=January 25, 2025 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=December 23, 1984 |page=191 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> The following month, it was announced that actor [[Jack Lemmon]] would preside over emceeing duties for the 1985 ceremony. Allen explained the decision to hire Lemmon, saying, "Jack's untiring energy, zest for living, and imaginative talents have won respect and approval of everyone in the film community."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Paris |first1=Barry |title=People: Jack and Oscar |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/pittsburgh-post-gazette-people-recap-new/166682886/ |access-date=March 2, 2024 |work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |date=January 31, 1985 |page=14 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] }}</ref>

In an effort to shorten the ceremony, ten actors ([[Candice Bergen]], [[Jeff Bridges]], [[Glenn Close]], [[Michael Douglas]], [[Gregory Hines]], [[Amy Irving]], [[William Hurt]], [[Diana Ross]], [[Tom Selleck]], and [[Kathleen Turner]]) were announced as "co-hosts" and served as either presenters announcing two awards each or introducing other presenters and musical numbers.<ref>{{cite news |last1=London |first1=Michael |title=Brevity is Key to Oscar Show |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-03-15-ca-35224-story.html |access-date=March 2, 2024 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url-access=subscription |date=March 15, 1985 |archive-date=December 30, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231230021255/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-03-15-ca-35224-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In addition, producers warned nominees prior to the ceremony that winners would have 45 seconds to finish their speeches before a blinking red light would flash and the orchestra would begin playing them off.<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=655}}</ref>

[[Marty Pasetta]] directed the telecast; [[Bill Conti]] served as conductor and musical director.<ref name="Pasetta" /> Oscar winner [[Theoni V. Aldredge]] served as costume designer for the ceremony which featured a segment showcasing the Best Costume Design nominees that included an elephant wearing costumes from ''A Passage to India''.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=Liz |author-link=Liz Smith (journalist) |title=Musketeers Break Oscar Jinx |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-south-bend-tribune-oscars-recap-by-l/166682632/ |access-date=January 25, 2025 |work=[[South Bend Tribune]] |date=March 29, 1985 |page=36 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> [[Scott Salmon]] served as choreography for the ceremony.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Howe |first1=Marvine |author1-link=Marvine Howe |title=Scott Salmon, 50, Choreographer For Radio City's Seasonal Shows |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/07/23/obituaries/scott-salmon-50-choreographer-for-radio-city-s-seasonal-shows.html |access-date=February 27, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=July 23, 1993 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240423105306/https://www.nytimes.com/1993/07/23/obituaries/scott-salmon-50-choreographer-for-radio-city-s-seasonal-shows.html |archive-date=April 23, 2024 |page=A19 |url-access=limited |language=en-US |url-status=live}}</ref> In view of the Academy nominating movies reflecting life in the American heartland such as ''[[Places in the Heart]]'', ''[[The River (1984 film)|The River]]'', and ''[[Songwriter (film)|Songwriter]]'', singers [[Willie Nelson]], [[Kris Kristofferson]], and [[Lonette McKee]] performed a medley of country songs.<ref name="Country" />

===Box office performance of Best Picture nominees===
At the time of the nominations announcement on February 6, the combined gross of the five Best Picture nominees at the US box office was $103&nbsp;million.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars>{{cite web |title=1984 Academy Award Nominations and Winner for Best Picture |url=http://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1984&p=.htm |access-date=January 23, 2025 |publisher=[[Box Office Mojo]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140329025512/http://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1984&p=.htm |archive-date=March 29, 2014}}</ref> ''Places in the Heart'' was the highest earner among the Best Picture nominees, with $31.2&nbsp;million in domestic box office receipts. The film was followed by ''Amadeus'' ($25.7&nbsp;million), ''A Soldier's Story'' ($21.4&nbsp;million), ''A Passage to India'' ($13.5&nbsp;million), and ''The Killing Fields'' ($11.7&nbsp;million).<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/>

===Critical reviews===
Television critic [[Howard Rosenberg]] of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' wrote, "The Oscar telecast was born to bore. It's unethical to tamper with failure. It's unholy. It's criminal. Now look what's happened. The Oscar telecast is good." He also noted that shortened acceptance speeches and well-disciplined production numbers made for a brisk-paced ceremony.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rosenberg |first1=Howard |author-link= Howard Rosenberg |title=The Long and Short of the Streamlined Oscarcast |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-03-27-ca-20280-story.html |access-date=February 27, 2024 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url-access=subscription |date=March 27, 1985 |archive-date=January 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250123153200/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-03-27-ca-20280-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Jerry Coffey of the ''[[Fort Worth Star-Telegram]]'' commented, "Monday night's Academy Awards show was the best in recent memory, a snappy, disciplined event that sacrificed nothing of value and trimmed off much of the obligatory baggage and extraneous clutter." He also commended Lemmon's performance as host while also singling out [[James Stewart]]'s Honorary Oscar acceptance speech as one of the emotional highlights of the night.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Coffey |first1=Jerry |title=Tighter Oscar Show, Without the Clutter, Best in Several Years |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/fort-worth-star-telegram-57th-oscars/76089989/ |access-date=March 12, 2023 |work=[[Fort Worth Star-Telegram]] |date=March 27, 1985 |page=8F |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> ''[[The Sacramento Bee]]'''s George Williams said, "It was a classy show all the way, a pure Hollywood production. Jack Lemmon, a two-time Oscar winner himself, was at the helm with his consummate timing and irresistible likableness."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Williams |first1=George |title=A Night for Outsiders |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sacramento-bee-57th-oscars/76089644/ |access-date=February 6, 2025 |work=[[The Sacramento Bee]] |date=March 26, 1985 |page=C1 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' television columnist Jon Anderson wrote, "Like a whale on a diet, Monday night's 57th Academy Awards ceremony on ABC-TV [[WGN-TV|Channel 7]] was leaner and trimmer than past shows, but seemed to have lost something. The show, still fat, lacked spirit." He reserved praise particularly for the Best Costume Design presentation and presenter [[Steve Martin]], but compared host Lemmon's hosting performance as "luncheon-club amiability" to previous year's host [[Johnny Carson]]'s "Las Vegas sharpness."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Anderson |first1=Jon |title=Oscar's New Diet Trims Fun Along With Some Flab |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-57th-oscars/76087187/ |access-date=January 23, 2024 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=March 26, 1985 |page=2 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> Michael Dougan of the ''[[San Francisco Examiner]]'' remarked, "Last night's extravaganza was more than 30 minutes shorter than the 1984 event, but not because the audience got less to look at." He criticized the decision to cut off various winners' speeches and several technical production errors such as flashing the ''Amadeus'' logo when ''The Killing Fields'' won Best Cinematography.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dougan |first1=Michael |title=Oscar Winners Slighted |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-san-francisco-examiner-57th-oscars/76089335/ |access-date=March 2, 2024 |work=[[San Francisco Examiner]] |date=March 26, 1985 |page=B7 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> [[Harold Schindler]], writing for ''[[The Salt Lake Tribune]]'', said despite the ceremony's shorter runtime, "It wasn't noticeably better, but it did provide plenty a copy for a TV bloopers and outtakes or a segment in 'Life's Most Embarrassing Moments' if ABC cares to use it someday."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schindler |first1=Harold |author-link=Harold Schindler |title=Oscar Show Runs on Time, But Some Big Goofs Still Surface |access-date=February 12, 2025 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-salt-lake-tribune-57th-oscars/76084031/ |work=[[The Salt Lake Tribune]] |date=March 27, 1985 |page=C7 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

===Ratings and reception===
The American telecast on [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] drew in an audience of 38.9&nbsp;million, which was a smaller figure compared to last year's audience.<ref name="Oscar ratings">{{cite news |last=Gorman |first=Bill |title=Academy Awards Show Ratings |url=http://tvbythenumbers.zap2it.com/2009/02/17/academy-awards-show-ratings/12818/ |access-date=September 5, 2013 |work=[[TV by the Numbers]] |publisher=[[Tribune Media]] |date=February 17, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109025135/http://tvbythenumbers.zap2it.com/2009/02/17/academy-awards-show-ratings/12818/ |archive-date=November 9, 2013 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> The show also garnered lower [[Nielsen ratings]] compared to the previous ceremony, with 27.7% of households watching with a 45% share.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/anchorage-times-oscar-show-ratings/166683614/ |title=Oscars Draw Poorest Ratings Ever |access-date=January 23, 2025 |work=[[Anchorage Times]] |publisher=[[Associated Press]] |date=March 30, 1985 |page=I-8 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> Nevertheless, the ceremony presentation received two nominations at the [[37th Primetime Emmy Awards]] in August 1984.<ref>{{cite web |title=The 57th Annual Academy Awards–Emmy Awards, Nominations and Wins |url=https://www.emmys.com/shows/57th-annual-academy-awards |publisher=[[Academy of Television Arts & Sciences]] |access-date=January 23, 2025 }}</ref> The following month, the ceremony won one of those nominations for Outstanding Art Direction for a Variety Program (Rene Lagler and Jeremy Railton).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Margulies |first1=Lee |title=PBS Shines in First Round of Emmys |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-09-09-ca-7099-story.html |access-date=January 25, 2025 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url-access=subscription |date=September 9, 1985}}</ref>
